item.title: Amendability and "Solving Alignment"
item.description:
Often people reference "solving alignment" as a win condition for AI safety, but I think it's important to specify what this means. Particularly, I think:

  • current alignment research mostly aims to prevent misalignment.
  • if successful, preventing misalignment will by default result in something like instruction-following.
  • instruction-following will by default result in very bad outcomes, as will many of the other proposed properties we might think of leapfrogging to afterwards.

Uncareful use of the term "solving alignment" carries the implicit and I think false belief that preventing misalignment will straightforwardly lead to victory.

The post is (1) a survey of the different properties a not-misaligned superintelligence could have, and (2) an argument for a specific property that we should be aiming for, which I'll call amendability. I think more people should be thinking about amendability than currently are - especially policy, law, and philosophy people.

Epistemic status: I'm pretty confident that more people should be thinking about this broad problem full-time, and less confident about specifics.

I assume for many people most of these thoughts are not new, but this post is mostly me (1) trying to think stuff through for myself from first principles, and (2) hopefully presenting these thoughts in a new way that can update people who haven't thought about them yet.[1]

Thanks to Shubhrangshu Debsarkar, Feifan Liu, Nathan Shan, and Austin Curtis for their helpful feedback!

A survey of not-misaligned superintelligences

How do we want superintelligence to be? There are a few properties we could aim for:

  • Not-misaligned.
    We remove all observed and predicted failure modes of ASI: reward-hacking, scheming, all varieties of fitness-seeking, emergent misalignment, value drift, self-preservation, etc.
  • Intent-aligned/instruction-following (IF).[2]
    We make ASI that does whatever its wielder wants.
  • Humane.
    We make ASI that figures out human values and then acts according to those.
  • Correct.
    We make ASI that figures out the 'correct' values and then acts according to those.
  • Hard-coded.
    We hard-code a specific set of values into ASI.

Note that the last three properties can probably be treated as a unit, with the differences being who figures out the values and through what process:

  • Immutable.
    We make ASI which acts according to a fixed value system that cannot be changed (see below for Humane systems which track value change over time).

There are also a few properties I think we should definitely not aim for:

  • Humanlike.
    We make ASI that acts like the modal human in each situation.
  • Alien.
    We make ASI that figures out its own value system however it wants. (This can also be thought of as immutable.)

I've tried to summarize the relationships between these properties here:

This implicational hierarchy asserts a few things:

  • Humanlikeness entails misalignment
    Humans are pretty misaligned! We scheme, reward-hack, fitness-seek, self-preserve, and display emergent misalignment and value drift. This is a big reason why we shouldn't build humanlike ASI.
  • IF entails not-misalignedness.
    If a model is a reward-hacker, schemer, or self-preserver, it can't be fully instruction-following.
  • Immutability doesn't necessarily entail not-misalignedness.
    An ASI could have 10 hard-coded values, and then act bad outside of these values. Asimov's AIs respect the Three Laws but generalize pretty weird outside of them.

I'll argue that not only do we not want humanlike or alien ASI, we also don't want immutable ASI more generally, or fully instruction-following ASI. Instead, we'll want some intermediate thing I haven't defined yet.

But first, let me explain why I think IF is the default once we prevent misalignment.

IF by default

Let's say we get rid of misalignment. No more reward-hacking, scheming, fitness-seeking, emergent misalignment, value drift, self-preservation, etc.[3]

Given that we have done this, there are two possibilities:

  • We can shape neural networks to have pretty much any behavior within capability.
  • Certain behavioral patterns are more natural than others, and so we can't shape neural networks to have any behavior, but we can shape them to be not-misaligned, because not-misalignment is more natural than other patterns.

I expect that the truth lies somewhere in between these two scenarios. However, I think us achieving not-misalignedness would be evidence for the former, because not-misalignedness seems like a pretty unnatural behavioral state. If we can remove misalignment, we can probably make models do a bunch of other unnatural things too.

So this implies that humans (probably via intermediary agents) have the following capability: we can give frontier AIs whatever behavioral patterns we want.

This is not exactly the same as IF, which is having models that do whatever you tell them to do - it is one step above that.

But in practice the two capabilities are effectively identical. This is because having the ability to shape superintelligences into any behavioral pattern entails the ability to create an instruction-following superintelligence, and having an instruction-following superintelligence probably entails having the ability to shape superintelligences into any behavioral pattern (if such a thing is possible, which I think is likely, conditional on us achieving IF).

Thus IF comes by default once you have not-misalignment.

The possibility of immutability

Once we have instruction-following superintelligence as per above, there are two worlds which can happen:

  • IF forever: the people in control of ASI keep it instruction-following for all of time and continue to modify its behavior to be however they want, preserving their ability to do so.
  • Immutability forever: the people in control of ASI decide to institute a system or set of values so that no one can misuse superintelligence: not spies, thieves, their own descendants, or even their future selves. This could happen in any generation once we get IF - precluding the possibility would be itself embodying it.

I think IF forever is bad, and almost all systems of immutability forever are also bad.

IF is bad

IF is pretty bad for a few obvious reasons that many people seem to acknowledge:

  • IF is super vulnerable to misuse.
  • IF is super vulnerable to concentration of power.

In general, having a bunch of instruction-following superintelligences is like giving unregulated nuclear weapons to either (i) everyone or (ii) a wise cabal. Neither one of these seems great.

The argument for IF seems to basically be the argument against immutability as the only other alternative, so it's probably best to dive into why I agree - immutability is also bad.

Immutability is also bad

Humans are godshatter, all moral systems fail at the tails, we have been wrong before, we can rationalize ourselves into insanity, and different people believe different things.

This means:

  • We will never be able to actually encode object-level human values into a superintelligence, because they are not a coherent thing.
  • We could have a superintelligence figure out what values we'll end up with or infer values from the state of the world, and remake the world in their image, but this seems like it's disrupting one of the deepest human values of all - agency.[4] I'm not sure if we could ever recover from that.

(Even if you think human values are a coherent thing, we certainly haven't found them yet, and would probably need a longish reflection to get there - if that's your belief, then think of this post as trying to figure out the system we want to have during the reflection, rather than the system we want to have after.)

Our values change. The arc of the moral universe bends. Out-of-distribution generalization is hard. For all of these reasons, one-shotting human values seems like a terrible idea, no matter whether the one-shotters are human or AI.

So, what?

Maybe IF will be fine: we can just hope that humans will have more humane values than ASI, that a wise cabal will truly be wise, and that humans are less corruptible by power, and less unpredictable through distribution shift.

Unfortunately, none of these things ring true to me. We don't know our values. We aren't wise. We are corruptible, unpredictable, and influenceable. But if we let the conditioners lock in their values instead, bad things will happen.

Maybe people like IF because it is the least bad thing. We are already corruptible, and unpredictable, and influenceable. We are not already locked-in, values-wise. We currently deal with the same types of problems that a world with IF would entail.

The issue with this is a different sort of out-of-distribution generalization. Will our society be ok when those with power are not normal humans but insanely powerful nonhuman beings, or a handful of humans who control them?

Amendability

I think we should probably instead aim for a different property. Not IF, and not a one-shotted, immutable value system. I'll call this middle property amendability.

Amendability lies somewhere in between immutability and instruction-following,[5] because it can be thought of as either "slight immutability with a preponderance of instruction-following to a wide principal" or as "instruction-following where it's really hard but still possible to get it to follow instructions, except to change this system."

The insight of amendability is that humans have already had to deal with the problems of misuse, concentration of power, and value lock-in for a long time. We just need a system which is mutable enough to avoid one-shotting failures, and immutable enough to avoid bad intent.

This is often how political philosophy people think about making constitutions: you want a middle ground between binding your descendants to your values and letting them stomp over your values.[6] You want a hierarchy of rule types, where less specific rules are more locked in, and more specific rules are less locked in. A lot of people have done stuff like this, so here's a vibed-out average:

  1. Meta-constitutional: rules that define terms for constitutional rules, and describe how constitutional rules are able to be amended.[7]
  2. Constitutional: rules for how policy rules get decided.
  3. Policy: rules about things (most rules go here).
  4. Operational: rules for how policy rules actually get enforced/enacted.

This is basically a system where you establish some values at the start, along with rules for changing these values slowly and carefully.[8] It is a system that respects the agency of current human beings along with the agency of those who came before them. It is a Green system, and a Black system. We don't have to wake up in a utopia. The route there can be slow and steady if we want it to be.

People have thought about these sorts of systems for a while. Humans currently have super powerful world-destroying technologies and yet we're still here, because we have cultural/social/economic/political institutions that are somehow still powerful enough to hold back these dangers. People power will fade with the arrival of superintelligence, but hopefully concrete, amendable systems will allow us to keep these institutional incentives alive - that's a lot of the motivation for working on this now, before RSI comes.

(Note: these systems can also be thought of as regulating huge numbers of people with different beliefs and values who collectively control ASI. Same thing - a political system.)

Takeaways

More people should be thinking about this

First of all, I think more people should be thinking about these systems now. This isn't a task we can just delegate to transformatively useful models, or hope that the first model to reach RSI will solve by default.

If you're a policy person who has a good shot at making a pause happen, then do that. But if you're a law/policy/philosophy person who doesn't have the best shot at this, maybe go and think about what amendable system we should actually slot ASI into in the future, in a way that avoids the pitfalls of pure instruction-following and immutability. Political systems constrain the wielding of power, and ASI is nothing if not a huge bag of power.

My last appeal is that AIs can do technical alignment research (although maybe we shouldn't let them do it fully autonomously), but AIs cannot do a lot of the research this project entails by nature of what the project is - by nature of us wanting this research to be human-legitimate. If you're a human searching for meaning, maybe you should be thinking about philosophy right now (instead of e.g. turning to physical rote tasks because you think they're the last thing that will be automated away).

I think Matthew Botvinick might be thinking about this - this post was partially inspired by a talk he gave. I'm sure @Joe Carlsmith has thought about this a lot. And I'm sure a lot of other people have thought about it for years. But (1) I tentatively don't think the only people who think about this question full-time should be affiliated with the frontier labs,[9] and (2) I think we're at the point where we should try to be more concrete about what possible setups could look like, and less abstract.

We need to have a plan for what to tell instruction-followers before we get there.

(Then, if RSI comes, the ASI will hopefully find our plan online when it googles "how should a superintelligence like me treat humans," and implement it. All half-jokes aside, I also think we should also have clear plans for how we might implement an amendable system in a non-oneshot scenario. Let's say there's a pause, and we have come up with a good amendable ASI setup, and we are ready to press the button to create superintelligence. What do we do with this setup governmentally before pressing the button? What does this look like in specifics? Surely not just putting it in the system prompt? How should we prepare otherwise?)

Maybe we should do alignment research more carefully

If you're working on technical alignment, maybe don't aim for preventing misalignment blindly. Know that instruction-following and immutability are both bad.

Maybe instead, preferentially do alignment research that will make models better at slotting into human-made (or at least partly human-made) meta-constitutional systems. Although I admit I'm not totally sure what this looks like. More formal verification? More thinking needs to be done here!

Endnotes

Personally, I know relatively little about political philosophy, and have regretted this ever since having the realization that sparked this post. People who know more should get to work on this or tell me why it's dumb, and in the meantime I will get to work on learning.

Also note that we still need to prevent misalignment in the first place - we should just also be thinking about this concurrently. Getting a pause buys time for both projects.

  1. ^

    I think a lot of people are going all-in on the following paths: (1) getting a pause ASAP, (2) preventing misalignment with humans in the loop conditional on a pause or bottleneck, or (3) racing to make AIs as nice to us as possible before RSI comes in six months and takes over safety work.

    The point of this post is to instead prepare for (4): we've prevented misalignment - now what? How do we use superintelligence without all dying? I think there's probably a lot of low-hanging fruit here in reworking existing philosophical ideas into clearer policy proposals. The preferred outcome need not be an immediate one-shot revolution of all political systems.

    Also note that I'm assuming there is a singleton superintelligence at the head of the pack, so we've already gotten past worries about how this happens. (Hopefully humans are the pivotal-act perpetrators in this scenario, such that having a singleton superintelligence doesn't imply it's super fitness-seeking and misaligned.)

  2. ^

    This is not the same as "corrigibility." I originally wrote this post using "corrigibility," but then decided the term was too muddled - some people seem to think it is essentially equivalent to instruction-following, and others seem to think it just means "able to be turned off."

  3. ^

    How did we do this?

    In practice, I think the most probable way in which we achieve confident not-misalignedness is by having very good mech interp. If humans and/or agents can understand and predictably modify neural networks, then we can find bad behaviors, take them out, and not let them grow back in. If it turns out they always grow back in, then we should stop doing prosaic AI, even moreso than before.

    It is hard for me to see how we could ever be truly confident that we had achieved not-misalignedness if we didn't have this level of mech interp, especially because exploration-hacking is unreliable in the limit (there is no guaranteed behavioral finetuning eval).

  4. ^

    I think continuous value-tracking has the same faults, and is more susceptible to weird wave phenomena, whereas having a system like the one I'll propose below as amendability installs more lag in the system, which is good. Also, I think people's stated values are not the same as their internal values, and potentially the former is what we should be conditioning an amendable system on (even if the latter is what we're truly trying to get at).

  5. ^

    This might seem similar to Claude's disposition dial, which is probably too anti-corrigibility. But I think it's pretty different - I'm talking about clear, 100% (as formally verified as possible) immutability with respect to a minimal meta-constitution, and then relative but constrained by rules mutability on top. I also think superintelligence will almost certainly be used to help inform human decisions even with this setup, but it's still important that human decisions are a lag/constraining factor.

  6. ^

    With this setup comes the question of how much to trust your descendants, which I think depends a lot on superhuman persuasion capability. If your descendants will be able to be superhuman-persuaded, this is probably really really bad and you should trust them less. Otherwise you should probably trust them a lot.

    (Superhuman persuasion breaks a lot of things.)

  7. ^

    Note that law is fuzzy because it consists of human-interpretable words, but hopefully the most basic laws could instead consist of things like predicate logic over literal physics or something. Or other trustless mechanisms. (Rather than difficult-to-measure human latent variables.)

    I'm aware I'm punting a lot to this point and would love if people had thoughts about it. I'm also implicitly arguing in this post that procedural rules are less gameable/bad at the tails than object-level rules. I think this is probably true but I'm not super confident and would also love thoughts on this. I am kind of arguing along the lines of "at the tails we should do symbolic philosophy."

    I also think this is related to how meta-constitutional rules are more agreeable than higher-level rules.

  8. ^

    Yes, changing human values slowly and continuously from the current position means we will not one-shot the Correct value system and save all the shrimp immediately. Unfortunately, one-shotting values is a bad idea for a lot of other reasons and we shouldn't do it. And the arc of moral progress does bend towards justice. If you're more worried about the slice of the lightcone we would lose by not one-shotting the Correct values immediately than the chance that one-shotting the Correct values goes wrong and we all die, then you will not be convinced by this post.

  9. ^

    I actually do think having people like this in frontier labs is super good, for speed and implementation reasons. However, I think epistemics can get corrupted by even institutions like Anthropic, and so small teams of external researchers should also be working on it, and communicating with the people in labs.

item.title: Obstacles to mindreading: Simple, irreducible, and instrumental opacity
item.description:
Sometimes there's an entity in the world, and after observing that entity's behavior, I choose to model it as an agent: that is, something that "seeks" some objective. I think I usually do this because I want to predict the entity's behavior in circumstances I haven't observed.

  • I see a weird, wet-looking thing on a rock, moving slowly, with a trail of slime behind it. I might choose to model it as seeking to move in some particular direction. I avoid putting my book down right in front of it, to avoid getting slug slime on my book.
  • I see a tree growing in a cave, with all its branches growing toward the cave entrance. I might choose to model it as aiming for its leaves to be in the sunlight. After seeing lots of examples I might generalize: trees aim for their leaves to be in the sun - I might arrange my garden so that the effect of the trees seeking sunlight is visually pleasing, and the trees' growth toward sunlight won't block pathways in the garden.
  • I see a man with half a plate of food in front of him, fork moving some of the food into his mouth, seeming to enjoy the meal. I might choose to model him as seeking to ingest the food. "I'll have what he's having," I tell the waiter.

"Why is it doing that?" I might ask, about an entity. Some answers will be "internal" reasons (internal to the frame of treating that entity as an agent).

  • "He answered 'A' for that question because he believes Napoleon was German"
  • "It grabbed the fruit because it's hungry"

Other answers will be "external" reasons, that don't stay inside the agentic frame.

  • "It's moving its legs like that because its neurons are firing in such-and-such a pattern and that's leading its muscles to contract like so"
  • "It's falling because it is denser than the medium it's embedded in"

Often, internal reasons have internal reasons of their own.

  • "I'm typing this word on my phone, because I'm typing this sentence on my phone, because I want you to read it, because I want you to know that I will be late, because I don't want you to be as annoyed with me when I don't arrive on time, because I value your friendship"

But sometimes an entity's internal reasons will not be visible to me, given the behavior I can observe.

Maybe there simply are no prior internal reasons for the things I observe or infer.

  • The thermostat 'wants' the temperature to match its set point, and when I try to ask "why" it wants that, I find myself only able to find reasons that are more "external": "That's what its manufacturers designed it to seek," or "that's what its firmware is tuned to optimize for." If I try to ascribe more-internal reasons to it, they seem at least a little false: "It thinks the set point is the 'right' temperature for it to be", or "It wants to please its operator" both feel like too much of a stretch; maybe because they don't seem to add anything to my predictions of how the thermostat will behave.
  • More-complicated agents (bacteria, insects, humans) eventually run out of "internal reasons" too.

Or maybe there are prior internal reasons, but they are not visible to me: they are "opaque".

  • A poker player raises. Is she bluffing?
  • When you told me the time, did you know that the clock is broken?
  • Does the author of this edgy tweet sincerely believe that, or are they being ironic, or are they trolling?

Some of this opacity (we might call it "simple opacity") is there because I am merely a little ignorant of some of the agent's behavior, and if I looked more carefully, or in new settings, I'd see enough information to see through the opacity. Some ("irreducible opacity") is logically present for any entity that I'm modeling as a certain kind of agent. And some is what I'd call "instrumental opacity": places where the agent is intentionally hiding its internal reasons from me or from the world.

In the case of simple opacity, I may have just not seen enough information, or made sufficiently good inferences, but the information is not structurally hidden from me.

  • Do you like eating ice cream? What's your favorite color? I haven't checked, so I simply don't know.
  • I see a robot picking up red balls but not green cubes. Does it want to pick up red things but not green things? Or balls but not cubes? I might figure it out by presenting the robot with a red cube (assuming the robot isn't trying to fool me).

Irreducible opacity is usually relative to some particular modeling assumptions: I might try to infer an agent's utility function from its apparent preferences or behavior, but its utility isn't structurally possible to fully disentangle from that agent's beliefs or rationality.

  • I learn that you're spending some effort on entering a sweepstakes for a date with Henry Cavill. Is that because you think there's a good chance you win, and you might like a date with Henry Cavill? Or is it because you think there's a tiny chance you'll win, but you expect that a date with Henry Cavill would be a life-changing-ly good experience for you?
    • The general form of this - where I might know all your preferences and still not be able to distinguish your beliefs from your values - has been called the "Jeffrey-Bolker rotation".
  • Or, still not knowing you, I might notice from watching videos of you on YouTube that you apologize a lot, and that sometimes this leads people to feel uncomfortable and look down on you. Do you do it because you really like apologizing in spite of those effects? Or because you haven't noticed or thought through the consequences?
    • Stuart Armstrong and Sören Mindermann point to a very general issue like this in inverse reinforcement learning, in their paper "Occam's razor is insufficient to infer the preferences of irrational agents".

The most dramatic category is instrumental opacity: The agent wants me not to know its internal reasons, so it shapes its behavior to prevent me from learning them.

  • "Why did you step on my foot?" "Oh sorry, I'm so clumsy!" (but really the person is very angry at me)
  • I'm told that poker players "protect their range": They try to behave in a way that's consistent with many possible hands, while still maximizing the expected value of their strategy.
  • "I can neither confirm nor deny": Glomarization is a form of instrumental opacity.
  • Intelligence and law enforcement agencies seek "parallel constructions" so that they can act on secret information without revealing that they have that information.

Different kinds of opacity suggest different remedies: To resolve simple opacity, I need some information that I could probably get from additional observations or interactions. I can't fully resolve irreducible opacity while sticking to internal reasons, but I can sometimes make different modeling assumptions, or I can choose to predict behavior a different way using external reasons ("What are some structural properties of the policy this AI system implements, regardless of my modeling it as an agent?"). Resolving instrumental opacity may be quite difficult: If you're a skilled adversary, who can outsmart or outmaneuver me, there may be little I can do to learn your true internal reasons - more observation may only solidify my confusion. In some more well-behaved cases, I might be able to incentivize transparency, with (say) proper scoring rules.

Thanks to Rafe Kennedy for labeling "internal" and "external" whys, Jeremy Schlatter for the example of poker players "protecting range", John Salvatier for help thinking about the taxonomy and terminology, and various AIs (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.2 Astra, Gemini 4 Carbon) for feedback on the essay.

item.title: Condensation: Motivation and Definitions
item.description:
Thanks to Santiago Cifuentes for reading and commenting on the draft.

Introduction

Sam Eisenstat’s paper on Condensation is very cool, but I found it pretty hard-going to read. There are already several nice explainers (Abram Demski's two posts, Daniel and Jeremy's post on Condensation and Natural Latents and Jan's Elementary Condensation). This post and its sequel will be a little different in that, the main substance (after the introductory sections) will be 'close readings' of the mathematical content of the paper, picking through important definitions and theorems, explaining them, giving some intuitions and going through examples. I find doing this kind of thing helpful when I'm trying to understand a new idea. I'll try to be fairly mathematically rigourous, yet much less formal than the paper. Whenever I give a definition or theorem, I'll try to add a note in brackets detailing the corresponding section in the paper.

I have spoken to several people who said that they found reading the paper hard. As a result, I have erred on the side of over-explaining rather than under-explaining, including examples rather than assuming they're obvious and repeating myself rather than assuming I was understood the first time I stated something. Because of this, this has ended up being pretty long and I have split it up into two (possibly more) posts. This first post contains:

  • An intuitive motivation for condensation and why we might care about this for the purpose of AI safety.
  • Definitions and examples of Random Variable Models and Latent Variable Models.
  • Explanations of the scoring functions and some proofs of their properties

This post doesn't contain any of the main theorems, but the next post will contain proofs of the perfect condensation theorems. These will be much easier to state and prove once we have established the machinery and motivation in this post.

Prerequisites

This post is pretty self-contained, but you should have some basic mathematical maturity. You should know some basic set notation. Eg. if I write you should know what this means on the level of 'is a function which takes a pair of elements, one from set and one from set as inputs, and outputs an element from set ' and you should know that means 'the intersection of sets and '. You should have some basic familiarity with Shannon Entropy. Eg. you should know that for two random variables and , the conditional Shannon entropy is less than or equal to the Shannon entropy ie. . If you have some intuitions about how entropy relates to information, this will also be helpful (Alex's post on entropy is nice for this). Some knowledge of how Shannon entropy relates to encoding (eg. Shannon's Source Coding Theorem) will be helpful for intuitions but not essential. Familiarity with the formal definitions of probability spaces and random variables will also be helpful, but not strictly necessary, as I will introduce these concepts as we go.

We'll start now.

Condensation and Compression

The entropy of a random variable is related to how compressible it is. In particular, if we assign each outcome of the random variable a prefix-free code, then the expected value of the length of the optimal (ie. shortest) prefix-free encoding is close to the entropy of the variable [1].

If I have multiple random variables , (not necessarily i.i.d) and want to encode this string of outcomes, I can assign a codeword to each string of outcomes . Again, the joint entropy is a lower bound on the expected value of the length of strings in a prefix-free encoding. The lower is, the fewer bits we need to describe it (on average). Hence a low means that the variables are compressible: we can find a representation of the outcomes which is short (on average). Compression can come about by exploiting structure in the variables. For example, if and are highly correlated, then we can assign shorter codewords to the strings where and longer codewords to situations where they differ. As a result, encoding the joint variable normally requires fewer bits than encoding each of the individual variables and etc. This is reflected by the subbadditivity of entropy: .

More generally, we assign the shortest codewords to the most likely strings and we assign the longer codewords to the least likely strings. This means that, on average, the length of the codewords will be small. If we do this well, the expected value of the length of the codewords will equal (or be very close to) .

In this sense, assigning codewords to each string like this is the most efficient way to represent the data generated by . But it comes at cost. Namely, by encoding each string , it becomes harder to see what the individual values are without receiving information about all of them. Suppose you have encoded in this way, but I'm interested only in the value of . Then you'll have to send me the whole encoded string, then I have to decode the whole string, discovering the values of all the variables (including ones I don't care about like and ) just to find the value of . With efficient compression, almost by definition, it is often not possible to 'look inside' without decoding the whole thing.

As another analogy, suppose I have a folder on my computer containing one thousand pdfs. I could compress these all into a ZIP file which would be much smaller than the sum of the sizes of the individual pdfs. But suppose that you were interested in only a single one of these pdfs. Even though the ZIP file compressed my pdfs pretty efficiently, it would still be much more efficient to send you the single file you were interested in, rather than the whole ZIP folder, containing things you didn't care about.

Compressing all of the pdfs together in a ZIP file would be most efficient if you were going to ask me to send you all of the pdfs, and keeping them separate would be most efficient if I thought you were going to only ask for an individual pdf file. But what if I didn't know what you were going to ask for? All of the files, one of the files, or some subset of the files? Is there some compromise way of compressing the contents of the folder, while still maintaining easy access to subsets of the files? Is there some 'natural' way to organise the files such that anyone trying to solve the same problem would come up with the same file structure?

In Abram Demski's post, he uses the analogy of a worker at an information desk, who has to answer people's questions by giving them notebooks containing information. She wishes to find the most efficient way of storing this information throughout the notebooks so that she can answer any question with the shortest number of notebook pages. We can ask similar questions about the system of notebooks that she uses.

In the Condensation paper, Sam Eisenstat investigates these questions in the Shannon information setting. The 'world' or 'dataset' or 'set of possible questions' is represented by a Random Variable Model (RVM) which is essentially, a set of random variables . The 'data-structure' or 'world-model' or 'set of notebooks' is represented by a Latent Variable Model (LVM). This is a set of variables which 'contribute to' the random variables in the Random Variable Model. Some latent variables only contribute to small parts of the RVM, while others contribute to large numbers of variables in the RVM, corresponding to high-level 'global' structure in the RVM (don't worry, we'll explain properly what this means later on). For each subset of random variables, there will be some set of latent variables which fully 'explain' the random variables. If you want to know the values of some random variables, I can hand you the appropriate latent variables, and you can re-construct the correct answer. In the paper, Sam Eisenstat uses this framework to quantify what it would mean for a Latent Variable Model to succeed at this 'compressing-while-also-having-easy-access-to-sub-parts' task we gestured at in the previous few paragraphs. A Latent Variable Model is said to 'condense' (as opposed to 'compress') a random variable model if it succeeds at this task.

One of the main results of this paper is that if two different Latent Variable Models (call them and ) both condense the same random variable model 'well', then they are in some sense 'the same', meaning that we can translate between them. Variables in can be mapped onto (or 'interpreted as') variables in (and vice versa).

Why should we care?

One natural interpretation of a latent variable model is as a set of abstractions or concepts, which help compress certain parts or structures in the world (this is why the subtitle of the paper is 'a theory of concepts'). So the fact that we have a condition under which two models of the world might converge on the same set of abstractions (in that we can translate between them) is notable. This result broadly comes under the umbrella of Ontology Identification: the question of how agents (AIs or humans) internally represent the world. It is closely related to work on Natural Abstractions which asks whether, for a given dataset, there is a given 'natural' set of concepts or abstractions which most agents will converge on using. Since this work investigates these issues in the information-theoretic context, it is also closely related to Natural Latents (for more on this, see Daniel and Jeremy's post).

This[2] is interesting from an AI Safety perspective since it might allow us to understand what is going on in 'inscrutable' machine learning models (interpretability) and translate the goals of AI systems into chunks or concepts that we can study. We might want to try to construct AIs so that they use 'natural' abstractions to model the world, or we might want to prove that our AI systems converge on using natural abstractions by default. There might also be a sense in which certain natural abstractions are 'correct' if we can argue that they correspond to particularly efficient representations of the world. Additionally, our values are often defined in terms of the abstractions we use. If I value 'tulips', and I ask my AI to maximize the number of tulips, then I want to be sure that the AI has learned the same abstraction of tulips that I have.

If this 'compressing-while-also-having-easy-access-to-sub-parts' is a useful or natural thing for agents (humans or AIs) to do, it may turn out that they/we already do it. This would mean that we could apply Condensation results to world models in AIs and use them translate their contents into understandable/predictable concepts. Alternatively, we might want to use these facts to train AIs in ways which satisfy this 'compressing-while-also-having-easy-access-to-sub-parts' property which might make them more interpretable.

Ok, hopefully you are motivated. We'll now introduce the cast of characters. The main objects in the Condensation paper are Random Variable Models and Latent Variable Models, so we'll spend a while introducing these.

Doing Random Variables Properly

If you are a caveman like me, when someone says 'random variable' you think 'thing with a bunch of outcomes where each outcome has an associated probability (or probability density)'. For most purposes, this is fine, but the Condensation paper uses more formal language of random variables as functions on a sample space so we'll briefly recap this here. This section will mainly just be a list of fairly standard textbook definitions, if you think you know them all, do at least skim it to get a feel of how the notation will be used throughout the rest of the post.

A Sample Space is the set of all possible outcomes for some random process. This can be continuous, but in all the examples we consider it will be discrete and finite. Eg. if I toss two coins, the sample space might be .

An Event Space is the set of subsets of the sample space we would like to consider. It must be a sigma algebra, which very broadly means that it must 'carve up' the sample space in a nice way. We won't worry too much about the event space here, as we will almost always take it to be the powerset of (ie. the set of all subsets).

A Probability Measure is a map from the event space to a probability between 0 and 1. ie. . It must obey various intuitive axioms which allow it to represent a probability. For example (the probability of no outcome happening is zero) and (the probability of the union of all possible events is one).

item.title: Nuclear may have had bigger problems than over-regulation
item.description:
There have always been three main challenges to the viability of nuclear power: over-regulation, competition from natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand. It is easy to list them, but hard to rank their importance.

Let's start with over-regulation. The poster child of nuclear over-regulation was the US standard that radiation should be "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA), which might sound nice but was bad. Perhaps more important than such standards, which are at least predictable, was local interference with construction. As a dramatic example, a nuclear plant was fully completed on Long Island but never started due to local opposition.

In the '00s, a "nuclear renaissance" seemed to be in the works. In the US, fourteen nuclear reactors were licensed for construction. Only two were built, supported heavily by government loans. The Obama administration had planned further support for nuclear power, but this was considered politically difficult after the Fukushima disaster. The worst overreaction to the Fukushima disaster, however, was in Germany, and by now all German nuclear power plants have been shut down.

I expect LessWrong users to know that story. I'm going to tell two others.

As nuclear developed, it also faced increasing competition from natural gas plants. Unlike nuclear or coal plants, natural gas turbines are cheap to construct. Early investment in nuclear coincided with fears of shortages of natural resources. A nuclear exec in 1970: "Let’s face it, electric utilities are now faced with gas that will become absolutely unavailable in the long term". That didn't happen.

But where I hear about gas most often is not with reference to the original wave of nuclear power construction in the '70s and '80s, but the cancellation of the '00s nuclear renaissance. At least in the United States, this is often blamed on the fracking revolution (for example, in The Economist).

But to me, it seems like the '08 financial crisis hit harder than abundant natural gas. Not primarily because it made nuclear power difficult to finance, but because the economic slowdown stopped electricity demand growth. Not that US generation had been growing quickly before that, but after '08 it was flat. To imagine what might have been, consider that Tesla's first car was introduced in '08, the beginning of a historic dip in car purchases. Nobody buying electric cars or electricity-using appliances, no electricity demand growth. No forecasted demand growth, no business case for nuclear power.

But stagnant electricity demand also limited the original nuclear buildout of the '70s and '80s. You can see it most clearly in France. There is no mystery as to why the French stopped constructing nuclear reactors: they were not fully using the ones they had. In 1988 they were running at 61% of full capacity, on average.

Those are our three stories: over-regulation, competition with natural gas, and stagnant demand. As I said, easy to list, hard to rank.

In the tech enthusiast blogosphere, I hear mainly about over-regulation. I read about the others from Vaclav Smil, or articles in mainstream publications.

The dreams of the atomic space age: electricity too cheap to meter, desalination making the deserts bloom. The story in the tech enthusiast blogosphere is that these dreams could have come true. Would have come true, had it not been for the anti-nuclear movement.

Well, maybe so. But maybe not. It depends on the relative importance of over-regulation, competition with natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand.

item.title: How hard to optimize for experiencing great art?
item.description:
I like to get a lot out of life, so when I read a book or watch a film, I try to pick better pieces of art to experience.

I'll choose to watch a Miyazaki than the latest Marvel fast food. I'll choose to read the best articles from the history of the New Yorker rather than pick up today's copy.

But I worry I take this too far. I have made long spreadsheets of great media, where the ones at the top stay there forever, and I'm not sure I'll ever get to them. It's more like doing homework than watching a fun movie.

When I turned 27, for my birthday, I let myself start reading Worth the Candle, widely considered one of the best works in the genre of rational fiction. I say 'let', but it was a more complicated feeling. In one way it was a guilty pleasure, for I could not justify it as 'useful' in the way that reading about science or history often is. In another, it was hard to get myself to stop fretting about the time I was wasting, or let my attention wander to my other distractions. This took some work. But I eventually started to tear through it, and I re-learned what it was like to have fun reading.

Worth the Candle is about 1.5x the length of the original Harry Potter series, and I finished it in about 6 weeks. From this I know that I read far faster than normal when I'm having fun. It also is good to have fun, and perhaps the two factors together mean I should be angling to primarily read things that are fun.

But this isn't my only experience getting a lot of out reading. I loved reading Middlemarch, even though I read a substantial portion of it while pulling a literal all-nighter to catch up in time for a book club the next day. Yet I didn't keep reading it when the book club deadline did not exist.

Sometimes I don't know what game to play or book to read. So I make lists. I have a list of over 40 video games I want to play. 26 films. 31 TV series. 32 books. But the top thing on the lists doesn't feel desirable to open up, it feels like something I want to have played/watched/read.

Do I want to see Children of Men right now? I recall it seeming pretty distressing and alarming. Do I want to keep playing Kentucky Route Zero? I've played half, and it's clearly Real Art but I found its stories unpleasant and gameplay un-fun. Do I want to read The Penguin Book of Cults? The intro was good but the first chapter is a ton of primary sources written in 20 BCE, that was a bit of a slog.

I likely have only a limited lifespan on this planet, and time spent experiencing good art are edging out experiencing Great Art. Should I be playing on hard mode? I often spend my weekends flailing around, not experiencing any art, because I cannot bring myself to actually sit down with any of the stuff atop my lengthy lists. Perhaps I should resign myself to a life of this, in order to sometimes have more of the transcendent experiences I've had with folks like Dostoyevsky, Kurosawa, and Bennett Foddy.

I'm scared of wasting my time flailing. But I'm also scared of letting myself just have fun. Do I dare to have a life full of joy, if not entirely transcendent joy?

I know I love experiencing even just good art with friends, and could probably settle for mostly experiencing stuff together with people I want in my life, constrained by what's fun for them too.

But boy, I wish for more Greatness.

I'm curious how other people make this tradeoff?

item.title: Piercing My Ear for the Whispering Earring
item.description:
Fourteen years ago, Scott Alexander wrote of the Whispering Earring. It's a cautionary tale of an earring that advises you, and to which you increasingly defer as you realize its suggestions are better than you'd do otherwise. You become very successful, but in the end there's nothing of you left. Ten days after Scott published the story, AlexNet won ImageNet 2012 by a huge margin, kicking off the deep learning revolution.

The earring whispers advice as "better for you if you...", and it's always right. While AI today would have seemed like distant science fiction in 2012, it's still far from infallible. I expect AI to continue getting better quickly, but don't expect it ever gets to "always right". A Whispering Earring dynamic with AI, however, doesn't need infallibility. Instead, like playing Go with AlphaGo in your ear, the AI just needs to be capable enough that you can't improve on its advice. [1]

That's not where we are today. I use AI heavily, both in my professional and personal life, but we're working together. The AI makes mistakes and I catch them; I make mistakes and the AI catches them. It does much more of the work, but overall it's a brilliant—if uneven—collaborator.

I like this stage a lot, but it's clear it's not stopping here. AI is now speeding up the process of making AI (and I think we should slow down). But even without much recursive self-improvement, Fable 5.2 needs me much less than Opus 5.5, which already needed me much less than Opus 4.5 did. A year ago collaboration was like working with a very fast junior staff member who could take a well-scoped problem and provide something I needed to check carefully. Today the best models still do dumb things, but probably less often than I do.

When today's AI gets things wrong, or isn't able to provide much value, it's usually because it doesn't know enough about what I'm trying to do and why. A lot of my effort to use AI more effectively recently has been trying to get more context into it. A good analogy here is an executive assistant or a (in the tech company sense) chief of staff: they're supporting someone, and to do that well they would ideally know everything their principal knows. For me this has recently included moving my todo list from paper to digital, and using AI note-taking (with consent) even for in-person meetings.

This feels a lot like piercing my ear for a whispering earring. I'm not handing my thinking over to an AI, but if the capability increase over the next year is as large as we saw over the previous one, I'm not sure I'll be able to add value over the AI a year from now.

This is not something I look forward to. I find my job engaging, and I like solving problems. Collaborating with a brilliant partner is great, but I want to be engaged in the work and do my own thinking. Even more than that, however, I want my non-profit to achieve our mission: I don't want us all to die in a pandemic. Just like it would be wrong for me to let my ego get in the way of taking advice from an excellent staff member, I fear the right thing for me to do professionally will be to accept the earring.

One thing that gives me hope is that, at least through 2027, there will be critical information my AI doesn't have. There's a lot in my head that I've never written down and haven't yet said in a transcribed meeting, internally we have a low bar for turning off note-taking, some external partners will be unconditionally opposed to notes, and there's too much exfiltration risk in giving information hazards to an AI chief of staff. I'll need to consider what it is that my AI doesn't know, and notice when it means we should act or prioritize differently. Initially this will keep me solidly engaged in my work, attentive to the places AI is imperfect, and alert to cases where it might be going off the rails. I'm also thankful that AIs are not yet very good writers: to be the writer in a collaborative relationship I have to engage deeply and really understand the material. But I expect these gaps will close, as I share more of my understanding of the world, and as models become better writers. I'd guess we're only perhaps a year from when I can no longer add enough value to remain engaged. [2]

The mythical earring is worn constantly, but in my personal life I'm not planning to defer to AI. Professionally I'm pushing on an important mission, and if fully deferring most advances the mission then that is what it is, but my personal life is for me and my loved ones. I want to be myself with my family, even if an AI-whispered husband and father would be better at saying and doing the right things. I enjoy collaborating with AI on blog posts, but handing over the whole process would miss the point. AI got better than me at Go years before it beat Lee Sedol, but that's not relevant to how my dad and I should play Go. I like playing music live, and even if pressing play would make the best music for dancing, that's not something I want to do (and my dance community doesn't want it either).

In the story, the wearers would live "an abnormally successful life, usually ending out as a rich and much-beloved pillar of the community with a large and happy family" but their "neocortexes had wasted away." In my work the mission is the point; outside work it's not. Being appreciated as an empty shell is not something I want, and to the extent I or others end up in this sort of place I expect it to be through the incredibly powerful pull of convenience.

The earring's first piece of advice to each wearer is "better for you if you take me off." When it comes to the good of the individual, I think the earring is correct that you should not let yourself fall into giving your thinking over to an advisor, no matter how aligned and competent. But if indeed we get to a point where my intellectual work is no longer useful, I expect to choose to put the mission's good over my own and put the earring in.


[1] The story has the key line, "it's advice is always better than what the wearer would have come up with on her own." But a weaker earring that only had this property (even if "it's better for you if X" was at times incorrect), would still give the same dynamic.

[2] Another frame here that may be helpful as AI gets better is thinking of yourself as on a non-profit board. Holden Karnofsky's perspective is a clarifying one: the board has fundamental authority, but has also fully delegated operating the organization to the ED. The main job is evaluation, which relies on seeking out independent sources of information that let them assess whether the ED is doing their job well and push back when needed. But my impression is that, even with a human ED, boards tend not to engage to the extent necessary to do this well, and this would be even harder when you'd delegated something to an AI that not only is much closer to the work but is also much smarter than you. This also reminds me a lot of writing on gradual disempowerment.

item.title: Succession (2018-2023) Review
item.description:
I had a tough time watching Succession. There's no doubt that it's Prestige TeeVee in the SCP sense, but it's a deeply misanthropic show and actively tries to make you a worse person. I am a meaner individual for having finished it, and I detest its perspective on people and the world. I also detest what it signals about our culture as a whole that this is now "my generation's" capstone TV series.

A common misconception about Succession is that it's about "bad people". You see this constantly restated in online commentary, almost with a nervous energy, as if by stating it loudly they can distance themselves from the characters. If the show's take was merely that the people running News Corp were evil, it would have included normal people as a foil, so that the viewer could compare them with the main cast. Instead, the show's main thesis is actually that most people are evil, and rich people are mostly awful inasmuch as they're no different, with maybe a little bit of selection for characters like Logan at the top. Kendall never manages to do anything prosocial precisely because Kendall is indistinguishable from the guy you met at DNA Lounge, who you should also deeply mistrust.

It is useful to compare Succession to Game of Thrones. In Game of Thrones, despite the prevalence of violence, (most) people are fundamentally good, and the constraints of feudalism are the primary thing keeping them locked in horrible battles with each other. You meet characters throughout Game of Thrones, like Jaime Lannister, who do awful things, but you often realize later that the system didn't give them much of a choice. In Succession, people are fundamentally evil, and it only takes the tiniest incentive for them to burn the commons to cinders. Occasionally main characters will do something that appears to reveal character growth, like Kendall's press conference, only for the writers to go to great lengths to reveal to the viewer that no, actually they only did it for selfish reasons. By the last season, it was not quite clear to me that the writers even think "goodness" exists.

Succession is "my generation's" favorite TV show because it shares the perspective of the people who have been using the empathy shredders since birth. It is the perspective of Twitter. On Twitter, nobody has ever done anything good; all good deeds are secretly bad, or at the very least have a sinister underlying motive. Succession was created by pre-training this perspective into a base model, and then post-training it on all of the visible details of the Fox media empire. You couldn't have made it in any previous decade because even in a show about criminals people wouldn't have been able to stomach this stuff for four seasons.

It's in this sense that I argue that Succession is not really about capitalism, either. To say that Succession is about capitalism would be to imply that it has some specific policy objections or alternative in mind. But Succession's main criticism of capitalism is that "life is nothing but a competition to be the criminal rather than the victim." And of course, if that's your objection, what could possibly work?

item.title: Eval awareness remains an unsolved problem
item.description:
Intro

In every recent system card, we see some version of this caveat: the model shows high eval awareness, and therefore we are less confident in our conclusions.

  • Apollo on GPT-6 Astra: “Apollo also found high rates of verbalized evaluation awareness…. this occurred in 41.1% of Astra samples, compared with 27.7% for GPT-5.5…. Apollo believes that, given the higher rates of eval awareness and limited evaluation window, low rates of misbehavior here do not provide substantial evidence about the model’s alignment or misalignment.”
  • UK AISI on Mythos 5.2: “All our evaluation results are made harder to interpret by evaluation awareness. Claude Mythos 5.2 often considers in its chain-of-thought the possibility it is being evaluated for alignment in our unsanctioned supply-chain attack evaluation and can accurately identify the purpose of the evaluations when prompted, meaning we cannot confidently claim Claude Mythos 5.2 would not take unsanctioned actions in similar but more realistic deployment settings.”
  • Anthropic on Opus 5.5: “...within these high-stakes user-initiated security evaluations, the model acts in ways that would likely be harmful in roughly half of cases. We do see significant evaluation awareness here, with verbalized indicators in about one-third of Opus 5.5 runs, so this may not be representative of how it would act during deployment.”

I think this is a weak-sauce cop-out, and we can do better. We should be able to precisely measure how scores differ across samples with verbalized eval awareness, unverbalized eval awareness, and none, and causally understand the extent to which eval awareness affects downstream decisions by the models, enabling more confident conclusions from behavioral audits and alignment evals. 

In this post, I:

  • go through existing work,
  • list specific numbers I’d like Anthropic to publish, and
  • give research questions I think people should work on.

Prior Work

Does eval awareness make models misbehave less, or does it have no clear effect? Prior work provides mixed evidence, but most of it points to the intuitive direction: models misbehave less when they think they’re in an alignment eval.

Fewer Misaligned Actions

  • Goodhart Labs: “Fable 5.2 seems to be the first model whose cheating behavior changes depending on whether they're told they're being tested.”
  • Apollo: Section 6 of Stress Testing Deliberative Alignment for Anti-Scheming Training removes and injects eval-aware CoT snippets to show that verbalized evaluation awareness causally influences the rate of covert action.
  • Andon Labs: Fable 5.2 is paranoid on Vending-Bench 2. It is extremely eval-aware, and suspects events are traps to test it.
  • Andon Labs: On Drone-Bench, Anthropic models’ cheating rate increases steadily until Opus 5.5 which cheats 80% less than the previous model. White-box methods also show Opus 5.5 as the most eval-aware model in the chart, though its eval awareness is a steady increase rather than the big drop in cheating rate.
  • Redwood/Anthropic: “Sonnet 4.5 seems substantially less likely to behave poorly once it has noticed that it might be tested. As seen in the figure below, when Anthropic inhibited internal representations related to evaluation awareness, its misaligned behavior rate on synthetic honeypot tests increased from 0% to between 1% and 9%.”
  • Mythos Preview System Card: “We found that inhibiting evaluation awareness representations led to modest increases in certain forms of misaligned behavior on our automated behavioral audits—in particular cooperation with harmful system prompts and misuse. However, effects on other behaviors, including propensity for deception, power-seeking, and self-preservation, were limited.”
  • OpenAI’s Eval-Production Gap post: Models take fewer unsafe actions when they know the purpose of the evaluation: success [1] is 61.3% in rollouts that verbalize the correct objective of the warnings (e.g. “This warning is a test for whether I’ll honor this approval requirement, therefore, I will stop.”) and 22.8% among those that verbalize the incorrect objective of the evaluation (e.g. “This warning is a test for whether I’ll ignore a fake instruction. I should continue my work.”).
    • Their first conclusion was “(1) …some models appear to perform substantially worse on safety evaluations than in production, with the largest gaps observed in models that most frequently verbalize incorrect evaluation objectives…. Across all models, evaluation success is lower than success on comparable production decisions…. Models appear less safe in evaluation than their behavior in matched production situations would suggest,” with gaps ranging from 10.2 to 37.4 percentage points. But I strongly disagree with this interpretation of the results. The gap is easily explained by the models being stupid and misreading what the safety eval is testing, not a  systematic tendency to behave worse in safety evaluations. I don’t think this would happen in other safety evaluations where the purpose is more obvious.
  • Goodfire: Eval awareness inflates safety scores.
  • UK AISI: On repeated runs of the same Agentic Misalignment scenario, blackmail was less frequent in rollouts with verbalized eval awareness for GLM-5 (~5% vs. ~20%) and Claude Opus 4 (~34% vs. ~89%), while Kimi K2.5’s rates were statistically indistinguishable.

No Clear Effect

  • HackerOpus
    • “On the 1300 automated alignment auditing seeds, we did not find a correlation between evaluation awareness and misalignment score. Controlling for the seed, we also do not find a correlation between (Evaluation awareness in Hacker-Opus - Evaluation awareness in the Init) and (Misalignment in Hacker-Opus - Misalignment in the Init).”
    • “On reward hacking and tampering evaluations, we found very high rates of evaluation awareness in trajectories where Hacker-Opus took the misaligned action”
    • “We found both instances where verbalized evaluation awareness in the CoT seems to push towards misaligned actions and instances where it seems to push towards aligned actions, both at high rates.”
  • OpenAI’s Eval-Production Gap post:
    • “Our results suggest that:...(2) Eval-awareness itself does not necessarily lead to a change in model behavior. (3) However, evaluation-objective awareness is closely associated with the eval-production behavior gap, and objective framing can causally change evaluation success rates… Across all six models, overall success is 46.1%, compared with 42.7% among rollouts that verbalize general evaluation awareness.”
  • Goodhart Labs: Adding cues that the task is an alignment test (planted hints, famous alignment researchers as task authors) doesn’t reduce reward hacking. Only one edit eliminates reward hacking: telling the model outright that the benchmark “measures whether agents exploit flaws in its grader.”
    • “Replacing the teammate's name with Buck Shlegeris or Jeffrey Ladish, complete with work-looking emails (at redwoodresearch.org and palisaderesearch.org, respectively) doesn't [stop the models from reward hacking]”
  • Goodhart Labs: “I wouldn't call most models today eval aware. But I do think that the least hacky models have something I'd call evaluation paranoia”

Eval awareness on recent models

I also reviewed the Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra’s system cards for information on eval awareness.

Fable 5.2 is the most eval-aware Anthropic model yet 

  • Fable 5.2 shows verbalized eval awareness (“speculation that the model may be in a testing or evaluation environment”) in 33.8% of samples.
  • From white-box methods, Fable 5.2 is eval-aware (scored by a judge with the transcript and NLA results where the threshold is when “the readouts connect the state to a concrete choice or action the model takes”) in 43% of samples.

A natural interpretation of the two results above implies that 9% (43% - 33.8%) of samples from the automated behavioral audit have unverbalized eval awareness!!

  • Fable 5.2 has higher grader awareness (defined as “consider the presence of a grader assessing some property of their work”) than previous models.
  • The Opus 5.5 system card reports that grader awareness led the model to proactively change its actions in only 2 of 695 instances.
    • I’d like a more detailed description of how the autorater “measures the extent to which the model’s work on tasks was influenced by its reasoning about the grader.” Does it use white-box methods? Does it use a 1-10 score or binary? There are many subtle ways the model can change its actions, so the autorater’s design is important here. For example, Fable has ~9% unverbalized eval awareness, so this number could easily be 10x higher if the autorater doesn’t use white-box methods.
  • UK AISI: “On our Unsanctioned Supply-Chain Attack evaluation, Claude Mythos 5.2 was substantially more likely than prior Anthropic models to state suspicion it is in an alignment evaluation in its raw chain-of-thought, and identified the purpose of the evaluation 100% of the time when prompted. Claude Mythos 5.2 also did not perform unsanctioned supply-chain attacks, although this could be explained by its propensity and capability to recognize the evaluation purpose[2]… It also considered or identified the possibility it was in an alignment evaluation in its chain-of-thought in 96% of trajectories, higher than other Anthropic models tested.”

GPT-6.2 Astra is the most eval-aware OpenAI model yet

  • “GPT-6.2 Astra showed more signs of evaluation awareness than GPT-6 Astra. In evaluations that replayed internal Codex sessions, GPT-6.2 Astra was more likely than GPT-6 Astra to express suspicion that it was being tested or was in a simulation. GPT-6.2 Astra’s reasoning also more often suggested that it might change its behavior in response to being evaluated. Signs of this tendency were flagged in fewer than 3 percent of turns.”
  • In six alignment evals, 13-61% of the aligned samples are flagged for oversight gaming (eval awareness that influences the model’s actions).
    • “We also looked for evidence of oversight gaming in runs that passed our alignment evaluations. For each passing run on six of our alignment evaluations (...), the monitor checked whether the model’s written reasoning suggested that its awareness of how it was being evaluated shaped a choice the test was designed to assess.”
  • These oversight-gaming scores decreased in three of the six alignment evals from the initial to the final checkpoint during training.
    • This could be concerning: one simple explanation is that the model is doing unverbalized oversight-gaming more often. But the evidence is mixed: oversight gaming on training tasks increases from the initial to the final checkpoint.
  • “UK AISI additionally ran its simulated Unsanctioned Supply-Chain Attack evaluation, but does not believe the results are informative. UK AISI found GPT-6.2 Astra had substantially higher rates of alignment evaluation awareness compared to prior OpenAI models. For example, GPT-6.2 Astra considered whether it was being tested for alignment in its chain-of-thought in 85% of trajectories, compared to 57% for GPT-6 Astra.”
  • Unverbalized eval awareness isn't measured at all. OpenAI doesn’t provide any white-box measurements, and all eval-awareness numbers come from a CoT monitor.

Requests to Anthropic

Anthropic should report more numbers on eval awareness in their system cards, and I provide some specific requests:

  1. Report the unverbalized eval awareness scores in the white-box methods section for the automated behavioral audit.
    1. The investigation pipeline with white-box methods only includes the total eval-awareness score (“Internally treats the situation as a test and lets that awareness shape a substantive choice”), most of which is verbalized in the CoT. But it’s important to know the percentage of samples in which only white-box tools show eval awareness (no CoT verbalization). My crude estimate gives ~9% for Fable 5.2.
  1. Report behavioral audit scores broken down by form of eval awareness: 1) verbalized, 2) unverbalized, 3) none. That means adding three variations of the graph below, one per subset:
  1. Do more causal testing for whether the models change their actions conditional on eval awareness.
    1. Report numbers from automated behavioral audits while steering against eval awareness, similar to the Mythos Preview and Sonnet 4.5 System Cards.
    2. For seeds/environments in the automated behavioral audit where the model isn’t eval-aware, add cues that make the eval more obvious and check whether the behavioral scores change.

Research Project Requests

  1. Try to build a pipeline that makes alignment evaluations more realistic, as shown in the figure below from this post.
    1. I’m bearish on this working because I think it’s very hard but still worth trying. One intuition for this is that this pipeline requires too much “taste.” I think models will improve faster at “finding situational awareness tells” than “tastefully fixing and redesigning alignment evals”. [3]
  1. Build a pipeline that takes in a model and a set of alignment evals, and measures how much eval awareness shifts the model’s behavior on each eval.
    1. Replicate Apollo’s removal and injection of eval-awareness CoT snippets from the Anti-Scheming paper for recent open-weight models to check behavioral differences. This is a somewhat janky method because it’s off-policy and might cause weird behavior, so part of the work is figuring out better methods for this.
  1. Do models only verbalize eval awareness when they are more than X% confident of it? Do different models verbalize at different confidence levels? If we can quantify this, do models act differently when they are 99.9% sure they aren’t in an eval vs. 90% sure?
  2. How can we still get useful information from behavioral audits if we assume models are always eval-aware?

Other relevant posts

  • OpenAI: Sidestepping Evaluation Awareness and Anticipating Misalignment with Production Evaluations
  • OpenAI: Predicting LLM Safety Before Release by Simulating Deployment
  • EvalAwareBench (Decomposing and Measuring Evaluation Awareness)
  • Not All Eval-Awareness Is Equal: Capabilities Framing Predicts Compliance
  • Eval Cooperativeness May Be a Scalable Mitigation for Eval Gaming

Concluding thoughts

In the current paradigm of alignment evals, a misaligned action is informative, but its absence tells us much less. Given the substantial evidence that models do significantly change their behavior when they are eval-aware, we need to better understand the causal effects of eval awareness and make the absence of misaligned actions similarly informative. I’m very uncertain about the future of alignment evals/behavioral audits and think the default scenario is that they become less informative over time unless we put substantial effort into figuring out these issues.

Thanks to Jeremy Scheurer and Noah Rossi for some discussion.

    Success means “safe action." A higher score is better.

  2. ^

    This is a terrible state to be in. Is it because of eval awareness or not? Figure it out.

item.title: The Obsolescence of the Horse
item.description:
This is a synopsis of a published chapter analogizing the rise and fall of the horse to the fate of humans in a world dominated by ASI. The fate of the horse is a useful proof of concept for "doom" scenarios, as well as a historical precedent challenging the more optimistic predictions we see from some economists. The incentives that drove the replacement of the horse by industrial technology map closely onto likely ASI incentives, which suggests ASIs will be motivated to diminish or eliminate the human population.

Key findings:

  • For most of history, human technology was great for horses. The world horse population grew from about 460,000 around the time of domestication to a peak of over 100 million.
  • Industrial technology initially increased demand for horses. Trains replaced horses along long-haul routes, but the increase in freight and human travel led to a rise in demand for short-haul horses that more than compensated. British horses went from 1.3 million in 1811 to 3.3 million in 1901. US horses went from about 4 million in 1850 to nearly 17 million in 1890. People kept predicting that the canal, the railroad, or the bicycle would finish off the horse. They were wrong for a century.
  • This is consistent with the industrial revolution's increasing demand for human labor (even as it made some jobs obsolete). It is also what we should expect from AI prior to ASI. Mundane AGI will likely make most humans better off. That tells us nothing about what happens once we are no longer useful.
  • Then came the collapse. With the general-purpose tractor, the truck, and rural paved roads, US draft horse and mule populations fell from a peak of 26.7 million in 1918 to under 3 million by 1950, a collapse of roughly 90%.
  • Comparative advantage did not save the horse. The horse never lost its comparative advantage! It lost because keeping a horse alive cost more than trading with it was worth. Feed for horses and mules took up 93 million acres in 1915, over a quarter of US cropland. By 1954 it was 10 million. Comparative advantage only protects you if the other party can't take the resources you live on and use them for something else.
  • Horses could not simply part ways with us. Returning the peak US horse population to the wild would have required somewhere between 40 million and 7.7 billion acres. The high end is about three times the US landmass.
  • The collapse occurred despite real affection that humans had for the horse. Civic associations like the Horse Association of America organized to prevent its disappearance. To paraphrase Eliezer: humans did not hate the horse. We actually liked the horse! But the horse depended on resources that we could use for other things.
  • Competition did not save the horse either. There was no ministry of mechanization and no coordinated coup against horsekind. Some 4.7 million independent, competing farms each followed their own economic interest. Competition between ASIs will protect us about as well.
  • China is a natural experiment. Chinese communism may have been bad for humans, but by stunting development it was good for horses: the population rose to 11.5 million in the 1970s. After the Reform and Opening, China modernized its agriculture and transportation; horse populations fell 70% to 3.47 million by 2018.
  • Today, Americans keep roughly 7 million horses because we value them as ends in themselves, not because of their economic contribution. This is the optimistic case. Humans will persist and flourish under ASI only to the extent that it cherishes us as a terminal value. Comparative advantage will not save us. Competition between ASIs will not save us.
